title: Pediatric Anemia of CKD: Iron Repletion, ESA Targets and Resistance
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology
module: Pediatric AKI, Dialysis and Chronic Kidney Disease

steps.say: Progressive loss of functional nephrons impairs erythropoietin synthesis and disrupts physiological iron regulation.
steps.tx: Evaluate the complex **Pathophysiology: EPO deficiency and hepcidin** driving anemia in chronic kidney disease. Anemia of CKD develops as functional renal mass declines below GFR 60 mL/min/1.73m², driven primarily by deficient production of erythropoietin (EPO) by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts, shortened erythrocyte survival, uremic marrow suppression, and chronic inflammation which increases hepatic hepcidin, blocking ferroportin-mediated intestinal iron absorption and macrophage iron release.

vis.alt: Hepcidin trapping iron in macrophages and restricting red cell production.
vis.caption: Hepcidin traps iron and restricts erythropoiesis. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation define thresholds for initiating parenteral or oral iron supplementation.
steps.tx: Assess iron parameters against standard **Iron repletion thresholds: TSAT and ferritin** before prescribing stimulators. According to KDIGO/IPNA guidelines, iron deficiency must be corrected prior to initiating erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs); iron therapy is indicated when transferrin saturation (TSAT) is <= 20% and serum ferritin is <= 100 ng/mL in non-dialysis CKD (or <= 200 ng/mL in hemodialysis patients), aiming for targets of TSAT > 20% and ferritin 100-500 ng/mL.

vis.alt: Duodenal iron absorption, macrophage recycling and hepcidin control of ferroportin.
vis.caption: Iron handling: absorption, recycling and hepcidin control. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Intravenous iron overcomes hepcidin-mediated intestinal blockade in children on maintenance hemodialysis.
steps.tx: Select appropriate routes comparing **Oral vs IV iron therapy in pediatric CKD** based on dialysis status. While oral iron (ferrous sulfate or polysaccharide iron complex at 2-3 mg/kg/day elemental iron) is first-line in non-dialysis or peritoneal dialysis patients, children receiving hemodialysis require intravenous iron (such as iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose) because oral absorption is severely impaired by elevated hepcidin levels.

vis.title: Iron Formulations in Pediatric Nephrology
rows: 2-3 mg/kg/day elemental iron in non-dialysis CKD
1-2 mg/kg per dose over repeated dialysis runs
High-dose single infusion in older children

steps.say: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are titrated to maintain safe hemoglobin concentrations between ten and twelve grams.
steps.tx: Prescribe therapy using established **Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) dosing** and target parameters. Epoetin alfa (initial dose 50-100 U/kg subcutaneously or intravenously 1-3 times weekly) or long-acting darbepoetin alfa (0.45 mcg/kg once weekly or biweekly) are initiated once iron stores are replete, titrating doses to maintain target hemoglobin between 10.0 and 12.0 g/dL without overshoot.

nodes.label: Start Epoetin (50-100 U/kg) or Darbepoetin (0.45 mcg/kg)

steps.say: Normalizing hemoglobin above thirteen grams significantly increases stroke and cardiovascular thrombotic complications.
steps.tx: Avoid full anemia correction based on **Target hemoglobin limits (10-12 g/dL) and risks**. Evidence from clinical trials demonstrates that targeting hemoglobin levels > 12.0-13.0 g/dL with high-dose ESAs does not confer additional quality-of-life benefits and significantly increases risks of serious adverse outcomes, including vascular access thrombosis, severe de novo or worsening hypertension, seizures, and increased stroke risk.

vis.title: Risks of Excess ESA and High Hemoglobin
rows: Rapid Hb rise (> 1 g/dL in 2 weeks)
Loss of AV fistula or graft patency

steps.say: Persistent anemia despite high stimulator doses mandates investigation for occult bleeding, infection, and hyperparathyroidism.
steps.tx: Investigate underlying causes defining **ESA hyporesponsiveness/resistance causes** when response falters. ESA resistance is defined as failure to achieve or maintain target hemoglobin despite epoetin doses > 300 U/kg/week (or darbepoetin > 1.5 mcg/kg/week); primary causes include absolute or functional iron deficiency, acute or chronic systemic inflammation, severe secondary hyperparathyroidism causing marrow osteitis fibrosa, aluminum toxicity, and occult gastrointestinal blood loss.

vis.title: Differential Diagnosis of ESA Hyporesponsiveness
rows: Treat occult infection and sepsis sources

steps.say: Severe secondary hyperparathyroidism induces marrow fibrosis that blunts normal hematopoietic stem cell maturation.
steps.tx: Recognize the detrimental impact of **Secondary hyperparathyroidism and marrow fibrosis** on erythropoiesis. Severely elevated intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels (> 300-500 pg/mL) directly inhibit erythroid colony-forming units (CFU-E) and promote bone marrow peritrabecular fibrosis (osteitis fibrosa cystica); controlling hyperparathyroidism with phosphate binders, active vitamin D (calcitriol), or calcimimetics dramatically improves ESA sensitivity.

steps.say: Oral hypoxia-inducible factor stabilizers stimulate endogenous erythropoietin production while enhancing iron utilization.
steps.tx: Evaluate emerging options including **HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHI)** for oral anemia management. HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (such as roxadustat and vadadustat) represent a novel oral class that stabilizes the alpha subunit of hypoxia-inducible factor; by mimicking the physiologic response to hypoxia, they stimulate endogenous renal and hepatic erythropoietin production and downregulate hepcidin, thereby improving iron absorption and mobilization without requiring massive exogenous iron doses.

right.title: HIF Stabilizers (Roxadustat)
points: Downregulates hepcidin to enhance iron mobilization
